name: Space station (ISS)
description: Long-duration microgravity outpost in low Earth orbit with a sea-level-like atmosphere.
considerations: Microgravity: no buoyancy, so flames rely on ventilation flow and diffusion for oxygen.
Typical ventilation speeds (~10 cm/s) sit near the minimum of the solid-material flammability limit curve.
Evacuation to a docked vehicle is possible but escape routes can be blocked (Mir 1997).
sources: Researcher's Guide to ISS Combustion Science, pp. 21, 31
25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir (NASA)

name: Deep-space spacecraft
description: Crew vehicles in transit to the Moon or Mars (e.g. Orion-class); no quick return to Earth.
considerations: Microgravity, small cabin and no rapid return: early detection and prevention dominate.
Cabin may be lowered to 10.2 psi / 26.5 % O2 before spacewalks, raising flammability.
Artemis II's smoke alarm showed how disruptive an alarm is far from Earth.
sources: Researcher's Guide, Spacecraft Fire Safety, p. 34

name: Moon base
description: Surface habitat at an intermediate, oxygen-enriched atmosphere to shorten EVA pre-breathe.
considerations: 30 % O2 or more is a 40 %+ increase over Earth air: materials become much more flammable.
Lunar gravity (1/6 g) adds weak buoyancy; no partial-gravity combustion data exist in PSI yet, so microgravity and 1-g results bound it.
Upcoming FM2 and LUCI experiments will measure flammability in lunar gravity.

name: Pressurized rover
description: Small pressurized lunar vehicle sharing the habitat's oxygen-enriched atmosphere.
considerations: Very small free volume: smoke and heat build up fast, so detection speed and suppression matter most.
Dense electronics and cabling are likely ignition sources (Apollo 1 wiring arcs).
Escape means a suited egress onto the lunar surface.

name: Mars base
description: Long-term Martian surface habitat, months from any resupply.
considerations: Mars gravity (0.38 g) gives more buoyancy than the Moon, but still far less than Earth.
No resupply for months: suppressant stocks and post-fire cleanup are limited.
Expected atmosphere is oxygen-enriched and reduced-pressure like a Moon base.
sources: Challenge statement (partial gravity, bounding microgravity and 1-g data)

name: Spacesuit / pre-breathe
description: Reference case: pure oxygen at low pressure, the most oxygen-rich crew environment.
considerations: 100 % O2 at 4.3 psi: Apollo 1 showed how fast fire spreads in pure oxygen.
Prevention (ignition control and material choice) is the only practical defence.
PSI tests reach at most ~85 % O2 (inverse flames), so this environment is a data gap.
